sceneHappening: The collection for the poor in Jerusalem: the generosity of Macedonia and the example of Christ
summary: Paul tells the Corinthians about the grace of God given to the churches of Macedonia: "in much proof of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity." They gave according to their ability and beyond it, begging Paul earnestly for the favor of taking part in the service to the saints, and they first gave themselves to the Lord and to Paul by the will of God. So Paul urged Titus, who had begun it, to complete this grace among them as well. "As you abound in everything, in faith, utterance, knowledge, all earnestness, and in your love to us, see that you also abound in this grace." He is not commanding, but proving the sincerity of their love by the earnestness of others. "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich." He offers advice: they began a year ago, so let them finish according to what they have. "If the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he doesn't have." The aim is not relief for others and hardship for them, but equality: at this present time their abundance supplies their need, so that their abundance may supply yours, as it is written, "He who gathered much had nothing over; and he who gathered little had no lack." Paul thanks God who put the same earnestness in Titus's heart, who is going to them of his own accord, and he sends with him a brother whose praise in the gospel is known through all the churches and who was appointed by the churches to travel with the gift. Paul is careful, "avoiding this, that any man should blame us about this abundance which is administered by us; for we take thought for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men." So show the churches the proof of your love and of our boasting about you.
whySettingMatters: The collection was one of Paul's biggest projects (also Romans 15:25-27; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4; Acts 24:17). The church in Jerusalem was poor, perhaps because of famine (Acts 11:27-30) and loss of property, and Paul saw the gift as a sign that Gentile believers and Jewish believers were one family. The Macedonian churches (Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea) were themselves poor and suffering, which is why Paul holds them up. Paul's handling of money is careful and public: he names those who will carry it and says that no one should have reason to blame him (8:20-21). He does not say "give to be blessed"; he points instead to Christ's own giving, and to the idea of fairness ("equality"), quoting the manna story in Exodus 16:18. "Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor" is usually read as the incarnation; some also read it more broadly as Jesus' whole life and death. The word "grace" (charis) is used for the gift itself, so the collection is called a "grace."

questions: The Macedonians gave out of deep poverty. What does that say about generosity and means?
"Not a command, but a test of the sincerity of your love." How can giving be both free and meaningful?
Paul points to Christ who became poor. How does that example change the way we think about giving?
Paul arranges accountability for the gift so that no one can blame him. What can we learn from that for handling money in a church?
